brief.topic: Can Collisions Slow These Ants Down?

s01: Two ants collide, turn around, and walk away.
Surely all that bouncing delays their escape?
Here is the puzzle.
Our ants are points on a ten meter stick.
Every ant walks at one meter per second.
A collision reverses both directions instantly.
Reaching an end means falling off.
How long until this stick is empty?
Before tracking every bounce,
watch just two ants.
Give them different colored badges.
In the real model they meet and reverse.
Now imagine ghosts
that keep walking straight through each other.
The badges end up on different ants,
but the occupied positions are identical.
At the collision,
exchange the badges and the two pictures match.
If we only care when the stick becomes empty,
identity does not matter.
Replace every collision with a harmless crossing.
This ant starts one meter from the left and walks right.
It has nine meters left,
so its ghost leaves after nine seconds.
The other ghosts need
seven, four, seven, and one second.
The last departure is nine seconds.
Bouncing can change which ant leaves where.
It cannot change the departure times under these rules.
Now imagine adding a real pause at every collision.
Would this trick still work?
No.
The immediate exchange of motion was the crucial assumption.
